item.title: Be the Worst Person in the Room: Career Lessons From a Jazz Saxophonist Turned Programmer
item.description: Seven career ideas from Chad Fowler's The Passionate Programmer, from why you should be the weakest player in the band to why your career is a project you can't plan up front.
item.content:encoded:
Here is career advice that sounds like sabotage: be the worst person in the room.

Chad Fowler was a professional jazz and blues saxophonist before he moved into software, and he built a whole book on lessons like that one. The Passionate Programmer is written for people who code, but nearly every idea works for anyone whose skills can go stale. These are the seven I’d keep.

1. Be the worst person in the room

Your skills drift toward the level of the people around you, so choose them on purpose.

Fowler picked up a rule from jazz guitarist Pat Metheny: “Always be the worst guy in every band you’re in.” Standing next to musicians he admired, he was sure he’d be thrown off the bandstand. Instead, his playing started to match theirs, the way you pick up an accent after a few weeks abroad. The reverse also held. In weak bar bands he played like those bands, and the bad habits followed him to better gigs.

There was a second surprise. He wasn’t as bad as he feared, and he had proof: good musicians only call you back if they want to play with you again, and they kept calling. Aiming for the bottom stopped him from selling himself short.

Share this: if you can’t switch teams, join an open-source project you admire or a local developer meetup, and spend time with people a level above you.

2. Practice should sound ugly

Practicing and performing are different jobs, and most of us only do the second.

Fowler remembers the music-school practice rooms: ugly sounds through thin walls, from players who were very good. Practice is supposed to sound bad because you’re working at the edge of your ability. Athletes do their straining behind closed doors, too. Software, he argues, is the odd profession where people practice on the job, in public, on the employer’s time.

His fix was to write software nobody needed, so there was no pressure to cut corners. The results were awkward, and he came to read the awkwardness as a good sign. If only elegant code comes out of a practice session, you’re sitting near the center of what you can already do.

Share this: pick one dusty corner of your main tool (he suggests regular expressions, a compact way to describe text patterns) and drill it on a throwaway project. Then read other people’s code the way a studio musician sight-reads a new score.

3. Treat your skills like an investment portfolio

Every skill you learn is a bet, and bets have risk and reward.

Fowler runs a thought experiment about three technologies. Learning COBOL, an old business language, was safe: work was easy to find, but it didn’t pay spectacularly. Learning Java early was risky, since few employers used it at first, but it could pay very well for those who got in early. Learning BeOS, a dazzling new operating system, was risky and paid nothing: it never caught on, and the developers who mastered it never got their investment back.

Then he adds a twist. Old systems don’t die, they get replaced in stages, and during the handover the old and new have to talk to each other. Young developers don’t know the old systems and veterans don’t know the new ones. That gap is a job he calls technology hospice: be the person still able to support critical systems after everyone else has moved on, and you hold the leverage. The risk is real, because one day you’ll be an expert in something that no longer exists. His answer is to move fast and find the next fading system.

Share this: draw a line on paper, newest tools on the left and sunsetting ones on the right. Mark where your skills sit. If they clump in one spot, that’s your exposure.

4. You can’t win on price, so build robots

If you compete on hourly cost, someone cheaper will always appear.

Fowler tells the story of early web design. When websites were new, companies paid thousands of dollars for a basic one, and he gives 5,000astheexample.Peoplenoticed,learnedHTML,andthemarketflooded.Soonthesamecompanieswouldpay5,000 as the example. People noticed, learned HTML, and the market flooded. Soon the same companies would pay 5,000astheexample.Peoplenoticed,learnedHTML,andthemarketflooded.Soonthesamecompanieswouldpay500. Offshore programming, he argues, injected a large supply of low-cost labor, and you can’t afford to fight on price.

Managers can’t easily measure how fast a programmer is, so they count what they can: cost per hour. That leaves three ways to produce more software: faster people, more people, or automation. Faster is hard to prove, and he doesn’t want to encourage the cheap-army approach. Automation is the one left. He points to the factory robots of the 1980s: everyone was upset except the people who built the robots.

Share this: pick one task you repeat, and write a small program that does it for you. Start simple and don’t worry about reuse.

5. The boring job may be the freest one

Low expectations are a kind of freedom.

When Fowler helped set up a 250-person development center from scratch, he hit a surprise. Everyone wanted to build new systems and nobody wanted to maintain old ones. Maintenance looked low-status and messy, and new projects looked like the road to promotion.

His coffee analogy flips it. Give someone $1,000 and ask for a coffee, and you’ll be furious if they return with neither money nor coffee. Give them nothing and ask for a coffee, and you’ll be grateful if it shows up and understanding if it doesn’t. Project work is the first case: well funded, closely watched, expected to deliver. Maintenance is the second: nobody expects anything flashy, customers stay hands-off, and a bug that forces a redesign of part of the system is just part of fixing bugs. For a creative person, that can be the more open playground.

Share this: next time you want to dodge the unglamorous task, ask what you could do with it precisely because nobody is watching.

6. Work like you only have eight hours

Scarce time gets used better than plentiful time.

The Extreme Programming movement, a style of software teamwork, says people should work no more than forty hours a week. That upset managers and many programmers too, for whom long hours were a badge of toughness. Bob Martin, a well-known voice in that movement, renamed the idea the eight-hour burn: work so relentlessly that you couldn’t possibly continue past eight hours.

Fowler’s argument has two parts. Tired people make mistakes that cost time and money, and projects are marathons, not sprints. And your hours behave like money: when you have seventy to spend, each one feels cheap. By day four of a seventy-hour week, it’s 10:30 a.m., you know you’ll be there long after everyone else leaves, and you start reading tech news. A hard stop makes you rank your tasks and attack them one at a time.

Share this: set a firm finish time tomorrow, list your tasks in priority order before you start, and see how much of the list is done when the clock hits it.

7. Don’t plan your career like a waterfall project

You can’t know up front what you’ll want, so a ten-year blueprint will fail for the same reason big software plans do.

In the old way of building software, called waterfall, analysts write huge specifications, architects hand down designs, and after months or years the result arrives, thoroughly tested and not what anyone wanted. A group of developers rebelled and created the agile family of methods, built around the assumption that change is constant. Fowler later realized he had planned his own career like a waterfall project: newbie programmer, architect, manager, director, on track to become a vice president or chief information officer. The more he succeeded, the less he liked the work. He was efficiently building a career he didn’t want.

The fix was to change it, and for him that meant returning to hands-on technology. He pairs this with a warning about value rigidity: beliefs you hold so firmly you never test them. Like a frog in slowly heating water, you don’t notice the change. Many network administrators in the mid-1990s swore by Novell’s NetWare. No single event ended it, and by the time they noticed, the water was boiling.

Share this: make two columns, career and technology, and list the beliefs you never question. Then ask which ones you would drop if the evidence changed.

The honey

Your career is the biggest project you will ever run, so run it like a good team runs software: get feedback from people better than you, practice at your limits, automate the repetitive parts, and change course the moment the plan stops fitting.

  • Spend this month somewhere you’re the weakest player.
  • Schedule one practice session that is allowed to sound bad.
  • Map your skills on the new-to-sunsetting line.
  • Automate one task you repeat every week.
  • Write down one career belief you’ve never questioned, and challenge it.

One caveat

This is a book of experience and opinion, not research. Fowler backs most points with stories from his own career, and the eight-hour burn and be-the-worst ideas rest on his reasoning, not on studies. His examples also come from 2009. The technologies he names, such as J2EE and .NET, and his worries about offshore competition belong to that moment, and technology hospice is a gamble he admits himself. Keep the habits and treat the specifics as dated.

Source: Chad Fowler, The Passionate Programmer: Creating a Remarkable Career in Software Development (2009).

item.title: Your Gut Feeling Is a Con Artist (and You're the Mark)
item.description: Seven ideas stolen from Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow that will make you trust your own confidence a lot less, and decide a lot better.
item.content:encoded:
Here is the most unsettling sentence I took from a 500-page book:

How sure you feel tells you almost nothing about whether you’re right.

It tells you something else: how smoothly your brain managed to assemble a story. That’s it. Smooth story, high confidence. Messy story, doubt. Truth is not part of the calculation.

That’s the thread running through Daniel Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow, the life’s work of a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. I read it so you don’t have to, and kept only the ideas worth sharing. Here are the seven that survived.

1. What you see is all there is

Your fast, automatic mind (Kahneman calls it System 1) works with whatever information happens to be lying around, builds the best story it can from it, and hands you the result with a feeling of certainty.

It never says “I’m missing something.” Information it doesn’t have simply doesn’t exist for it. Kahneman’s abbreviation for this is WYSIATI: what you see is all there is.

The experiment that made me wince: people read a legal case, then heard from a lawyer for one side only. They were told they were hearing one side. They could have easily imagined the other lawyer’s pitch. Still, they were more confident in their verdicts than people who heard both sides.

Less information, more confidence. A thin story is easier to make coherent than a rich one.

Share this: when you feel certain, ask “what would I need to know that I don’t know?” Then go find it before you decide.

2. You rarely answer the question you were asked

When a question is hard, your mind quietly swaps it for an easier one and answers that, without telling you.

  • How happy are you with your life? becomes What’s my mood right now?
  • Will this candidate be a good leader? becomes Does she look like a leader?
  • How popular will the president be in six months? becomes How popular is the president today?

You don’t feel the swap. The answer arrives fast and fluent, so it feels like an answer to the real question.

Share this: for any big judgment, write the actual question down. Then ask: “Is this really what I’m answering?”

3. Confidence is a feeling, not evidence

Early in his career, Kahneman helped evaluate soldiers for officer training in the Israeli army. He and his colleagues watched candidates tackle an obstacle course and felt they could see each man’s true character. Then every few months they’d get feedback: their predictions were barely better than guessing.

It changed nothing. The next batch arrived, they watched them haul a log over a wall, and the certainty came right back, as vivid as before.

He named it the illusion of validity: you can know, as a statistic, that your judgments are poor, and still feel that this specific judgment is solid. Like the Müller-Lyer lines, knowing the trick doesn’t make it go away.

Share this: high confidence from someone (including you) mostly proves they’ve told themselves a coherent story. Treat admitted uncertainty as the more informative signal.

4. A dumb formula beats the smart expert

Paul Meehl dared to compare trained clinicians against simple statistical rules. The rules won, and kept winning. After roughly 200 studies, about 60% show the algorithm clearly more accurate, and the rest are ties. Predicting parole violations, business success, cancer survival, college grades. Kahneman notes that no exception has been convincingly documented.

Why do experts lose?

  • They try to be clever and combine many factors, and complexity usually hurts.
  • They are wildly inconsistent. Experienced radiologists contradict their own reading of the same X-ray about 20% of the time.

An economist built a three-variable weather formula that predicts the future price of Bordeaux wine better than the tasters do. And the best-known success story of all is the Apgar score: five quick checks, scored 0 to 2, that replaced gut feel in delivery rooms and, in Kahneman’s telling, has saved the lives of hundreds of thousands of infants.

Even a back-of-the-envelope formula with equal weights often competes with fancy statistics. One of Kahneman’s favorite examples: predict a marriage with how often you make love minus how often you quarrel.

Share this: for hiring, investing, prioritizing, anything repeated, pick 4 to 6 relevant criteria, score each one separately, add them up, and let the total decide. Use your gut to collect the scores, not to overrule the sum.

5. The test for when to trust intuition

Kahneman isn’t saying all intuition is garbage. He spent years arguing with Gary Klein, who studied firefighters that sensed a floor was about to collapse. They finally agreed on a two-part test. Trust an expert’s gut only if:

  1. The environment is regular enough to be predictable, and
  2. They’ve had long practice with fast, clear feedback.

Chess players, nurses, firefighters, anesthesiologists pass. Stock pickers and long-range political pundits fail, because their world offers no stable patterns to learn. Some environments are worse than useless: Kahneman retells the story of a doctor who “predicted” typhoid in patients. He was accurate, because he was spreading it himself with unwashed hands.

And the line I keep repeating to myself: don’t trust anyone, yourself included, to tell you how much to trust their judgment. Judge the environment and the feedback loop, not the confidence.

Share this: before you defer to an expert (or to your own hunch), ask two questions. Is this a world with stable patterns? Did this person get quick, honest feedback in it?

6. Your plan is a best-case fantasy, so imagine the funeral first

Plans are written from the inside: our team, our scenario, our enthusiasm. Kahneman calls the result the planning fallacy, forecasts hugging the best case instead of the track record of similar projects.

The receipts:

  • Scotland’s new parliament building: estimated at up to £40 million, finished at around £431 million.
  • Rail projects worldwide: ridership overestimated by 106% on average, costs overrun by 45%.
  • Home kitchen remodels: owners expected to pay about 18,658andpaidabout18,658 and paid about 18,658andpaidabout38,769.

Two fixes:

  • The outside view. Ignore your story. Look up how similar projects actually went, and start your estimate there.
  • The premortem (Klein’s idea). Before committing, gather the team and say: “Imagine it’s a year from now. We did this. It was a disaster. Write the history of why.” It works because it makes doubt socially safe. Once a group has decided, dissent starts to look like disloyalty. The premortem makes dissent the assignment.

Share this: run a ten-minute premortem on your next big decision. Then multiply your timeline by whatever similar projects actually took.

7. You’re two people, and the wrong one is running your life

Kahneman splits you into an experiencing self (the one who feels each moment) and a remembering self (the one who keeps score afterward). They disagree, and the remembering self gets the vote.

In a colonoscopy study, patients reported their pain minute by minute. Afterward, they rated the whole ordeal, and their ratings ignored how long it lasted. What mattered was the worst moment and the final moment: the peak-end rule, plus duration neglect. A patient with an 8-minute procedure that ended painfully remembered it as worse than a patient whose procedure was three times longer but tapered off gently.

The same distortion shapes how we judge our lives. Kahneman’s focusing illusion: whatever you’re thinking about seems far more important than it really is. People assume sunny California must make you happier. It doesn’t, because Californians hardly think about the weather. The same trap makes us overestimate how much a new car, house, or gadget will improve our daily lives, and underrate things like friendships and hobbies that keep demanding our attention.

Share this: end experiences well, because the ending is what gets remembered. And before a big purchase or move, ask: “How often will I actually be thinking about this?”

The honey

If you only keep one thing:

Your mind is a story machine. It values coherence over completeness, ease over accuracy, and confidence over evidence.

You can’t switch that machine off, and Kahneman is clear that even he never fully escaped its tricks. But you can build around it:

  • Look for what’s missing.
  • Name the real question.
  • Distrust the feeling of certainty.
  • Let simple formulas make the repeated calls.
  • Check whether the environment lets anyone have real expertise.
  • Run the premortem.
  • Plan for the memory, and for the attention, not just the moment.

The goal isn’t to stop having a gut. It’s to stop letting your gut cross-examine itself and rule that it’s innocent.

One honest caveat: some findings in the book, especially around social priming, have not held up well in replication, and I left those out on purpose. The ideas above rest on far firmer ground.

Source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).
